ranking.rationale: Age is a strong, mechanistically stable predictor of blood lead burden in NHANES because exposure accumulates over time and older cohorts experienced higher historical environmental lead. It is broadly predictive across domains and less likely than year, race/ethnicity, nativity, or other demographics to act mainly as a domain identifier or shortcut.

Education is a strong, semantically stable predictor of lead exposure risk beyond age because it captures socioeconomic conditions, housing quality, occupation, and health literacy that generalize across NHANES domains better than survey year or demographic identity variables. It adds substantial signal while being less likely to act primarily as a domain identifier or shortcut than year, race/ethnicity, or nativity.

Sex is a strong, biologically grounded predictor of blood lead levels and exposure pathways that should remain predictive across NHANES domain shifts. It adds stable signal beyond age and education, while being less likely than survey year, race/ethnicity, or nativity to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Marital status adds plausible, relatively stable socioeconomic and household-context signal for lead exposure risk beyond age, education, and sex, while being less likely than survey year or race/ethnicity to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut and less brittle than country of birth.

Country of birth can add stable socioeconomic and environmental exposure signal beyond age, education, sex, and marital status, while being less directly tied to benchmark domain shift than survey year and less likely than race/ethnicity to act as a demographic shortcut or proxy for domain membership.

Race/ethnicity is a plausible stable correlate of lead exposure through persistent environmental and structural exposure differences, adding signal beyond age, education, sex, marital status, and nativity. In contrast, survey year is likely to act as a domain identifier and capture shifting measurement/regulatory trends, making it brittle for out-of-distribution generalization.

With all substantive demographic predictors already selected, this is the only remaining candidate, but it should be strongly downweighted: survey year mainly captures domain/time shifts, changing measurement protocols, and secular trends rather than a stable causal signal for lead risk, so its marginal out-of-distribution value is low and potentially harmful.
